readerTitle: Airbnb's cereal boxes: money that buys time vs. proof that works
caseNote: 실제 기업 (Airbnb 초기, 2008~2009년 시리얼 판매와 Y Combinator 합류) + 일화 (Paul Graham의 반응) + 가상 적용 (B2B 컨설팅)
insight: 시간을 벌어 주는 돈과 아이디어가 맞다는 증거는 다르다. 버티는 데 쓴 돈은 실험할 시간을 줄 뿐, 그 실험을 대신하지 않는다.
misconception: 돈이 들어오면 사업이 검증된 것이다. 또는 본업과 상관없는 일로 돈을 버는 것은 무조건 한눈팔기다.

sources.text: Gallagher, L. (2017). The Airbnb Story. Houghton Mifflin Harcourt. (시리얼 판매, 부채, Y Combinator 합류 과정)
Graham, P. (2013). Do Things That Don't Scale. (Airbnb 창업자들의 뉴욕 호스트 방문)
Joe Gebbia 인터뷰, NPR How I Built This (Airbnb 편)
Brian Chesky의 공개 강연·인터뷰 (시리얼 박스 가격과 판매액 언급)

factChecks.note: 시리얼 이름 "Obama O's", "Cap'n McCain's"와 2008년 미국 대선 시기 판매는 널리 보도된 내용입니다. 출판 전 Gallagher(2017)로 다시 확인하세요.
박스당 $40, 총 약 $30,000은 창업자 인터뷰에서 자주 인용되는 수치입니다. 자료마다 조금씩 다르므로 카드에는 "about $30,000"으로 적었습니다. 제작 수량(약 1,000박스 설)은 확인이 어려워 카드에서 뺐습니다.
창업자들의 신용카드 부채 금액은 자료마다 달라 수치 없이 "credit card debt"로만 적었습니다.
Paul Graham이 아이디어보다 창업자들의 끈질김에 끌렸다는 이야기는 여러 자료에 나오지만 정확한 발언은 버전이 다양합니다. 직접 인용 없이 일화로 표시해 의역했습니다.
Y Combinator 합류 시점(2009년 초, Winter 2009 배치)과 뉴욕 호스트 방문·사진 개선은 Graham(2013) 등에서 확인하세요.

cards.title: The air-mattress startup that sold breakfast cereal
body: In 2008, the founders of a small website for renting out air mattresses were broke and in credit card debt.
So they made cereal. That website became Airbnb. But the cereal didn't prove the idea worked. It did something else.

image.label: Hand-designed cereal boxes stacked next to an air mattress
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 작은 아파트 바닥에 공기 매트리스가 있고, 옆에 직접 디자인한 듯한 시리얼 박스가 쌓여 있음. 실제 로고, 실존 정치인 얼굴이나 캐릭터는 쓰지 않고 별·줄무늬 같은 일반적인 선거 분위기 패턴만 사용.

cards.title: Few bookings, growing debt. What now?
body: It's late 2008. Your site lets people rent a spare bed to travelers. A few bookings come in around big events, then they dry up. You've built up credit card debt, and investors aren't interested.
You're designers. What would you do?

options.text: Pause the startup and take jobs to pay off the debt
options.feedback: You protect yourself financially. But the startup may quietly die, and any momentum you had is lost.

options.text: Make and sell something unrelated that uses your skills, to raise cash fast
options.feedback: You keep going without outside money. But you spend time and energy on something that isn't the business.

options.text: Keep spending on the site and hope bookings pick up
options.feedback: You stay focused. But debt keeps growing, and hope doesn't tell you when to stop.

choice.afterReveal: The founders chose something close to B. What it bought them, and what it didn't, is the point of this lesson.

cards.title: Obama O's and Cap'n McCain's
body: During the 2008 U.S. election, the founders designed election-themed cereal boxes and sold them as collectibles for **$40 a box**.
The boxes got press attention and sold. By the founders' own account, they raised about $30,000, enough to deal with their debts and keep going.
Notice what they used: their design skills and their nerve. Not their website.

image.label: A cereal box priced at $40 next to a plain store box
image.brief: 두 시리얼 박스 비교. 왼쪽은 평범한 마트 시리얼, 오른쪽은 한정판처럼 번호가 붙은 디자인 박스에 "$40" 태그. 실제 브랜드 로고와 실존 인물 얼굴 없이 일반적인 패턴으로.

cards.title: The cereal didn't fix the business.
body: Selling cereal said nothing about whether travelers wanted to sleep in strangers' homes. Bookings on the site were still weak.

What the cereal did was keep the founders alive, and show something about them. In a story often told about Y Combinator, a startup program, partner Paul Graham reportedly wasn't sold on the idea but was struck by founders this hard to stop.
They joined Y Combinator in early 2009.

cards.title: Runway is not proof.
body: **Runway** is how long you can keep going before the money runs out. Any cash extends it: savings, a side job, a loan, cereal.
**Evidence** is different. It's a sign that customers want the thing you're actually building.
Founders often blur the two. Money coming in feels like progress. But runway only buys you more tries. It doesn't tell you whether any of them will work.

image.label: A runway extending, with a separate gauge labeled evidence
image.brief: 인포그래픽. 왼쪽에 시리얼 박스가 활주로를 늘리는 모습("Runway: more time"), 오른쪽에 아직 바늘이 낮은 계기판("Evidence: do customers want it?"). 두 요소가 서로 연결되지 않았음을 보여줌.

cards.title: Then they went back to the real problem.
body: With time bought, the founders worked on the business itself. Paul Graham later wrote that they flew to New York, met their hosts in person and helped improve their listings, including better photos.
That was the work that produced evidence: watching real hosts and guests, and fixing what stopped bookings.
The cereal paid for the search. It wasn't the search.

cards.title: Two traps in this story
body: **Survivor stories mislead.** We remember the cereal because Airbnb became huge. Many founders have funded themselves with side projects and still failed. The cereal didn't cause the success.
**Side income can take over.** A project that pays the bills can slowly eat the time meant for the real business. Decide in advance how long the runway is for, and what you'll test with it.
cards.softwareNote: Many software startups fund themselves with consulting. It works when the client work teaches you about your users. It fails when the consulting quietly becomes the company.

cards.title: Now it's a small consultancy.
body: Your two-person firm is launching a fixed-price HR audit for small businesses. After two months, only two clients have bought it.
To pay the bills, you run a one-day management workshop. It sells out. Your partner says: "Clients love us. Let's push the audit harder." What does the workshop tell you?

options.text: It proves there's demand for the audit
options.feedback: It proves people trust you and buy workshops. Treating it as audit demand could keep you pushing a product nobody has asked for.

options.text: It buys time. Set a deadline and a clear test for the audit
options.feedback: You use the cash as runway and still demand real evidence for the audit. You give up the comfort of feeling validated.

options.text: Drop the audit and switch to workshops
options.feedback: The workshop may be a real signal worth testing. But switching after one sold-out day trades one untested bet for another.

cards.title: Money that buys time is not proof the idea works.
body: Airbnb's cereal kept the founders alive. The evidence came later, from working with real hosts.
**Try it today:** list where your last three months of income came from. Mark each source "runway" or "evidence for the main idea." Which column is longer?
